panels.figure_caption: Microscopic evaluation of lung tissues. Panel a, histologic image (Hematoxilin-Eosin, 20X) of lung autoptic sample showing widespread proliferation of septal capillaries with extensive alveolar hemorrhage, without a proliferation in septal, or lung bronchovascular bundles. Panel b, CD31 endothelial immunostaining (20X) demonstrates marked septal capillaries dilatation and proliferation
in_text_mentions: Histopathological analysis of the lungs showed marks of PCH (Fig. 1, panel a). Sections of the lung reveal lobular architecture with acinar underdevelopment and numerous dilated vascular channels within the thickened septa. Reduced radial-alveolar count was detected, reflective of decreased alveolarization. Air-blood barriers were detected within the alveolar walls; however, a rich, congested, proliferated capillary network was present within interalveolar septa. This is associated with some hemorrhage into the airspace as well as some regions with large number of hystiocytes in the airspaces.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Low-power H&E histology demonstrating excessive capillary proliferation and dilated vessels with hemorrhage in lung parenchyma, consistent with PCH. B: Higher-power H&E histology showing dilated vessels within alveolar septa, reflecting capillary proliferation characteristic of PCH. C: CD34 immunohistochemistry confirming proliferating capillary endothelium in lung tissue, supporting the diagnosis of pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis. D: High-power H&E showing excessive interstitial capillary hyperplasia and hemosiderin-containing macrophages, described as PCH-like foci in this case.

(C) Immunohistochemical staining for CD34, an endothelial cell marker, supports the proliferation of capillary (×200). (D) The excessive interstitial capillary hyperplasia and hemosiderin-containing macrophages were observed in high power view, which is compatible with pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis (PCH)-like foci (×400).

panels.rationale: This is a single, clear patient chest radiograph from an adolescent case report specifically diagnosed as pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis. The captioned arrow directly identifies marked main pulmonary artery dilatation, a supported manifestation. Although the corresponding vocabulary finding is categorized as CT, the same specified manifestation is visibly demonstrated here on radiography.

plate_findings.evidence: severe RV hypertrophy and RV dilation

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Echocardiogram from a 6-month-old patient with pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis showing severe right ventricular hypertrophy and dilation secondary to pulmonary hypertension. B: Echocardiogram from the same patient showing increased RV/LV ratio indicating right ventricular enlargement due to pulmonary hypertension from pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis. C: Chest CT from the patient demonstrating mosaic perfusion, a characteristic imaging finding in pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis, along with atelectasis.
panels.attribution_text: Hasan et al. Case report: Rescue treatment with add-on selexipag in a preterm infant with suprasystemic pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis, and isolated pulmonary vein stenosis.. Frontiers in cardiovascular medicine 2022. doi:10.3389/fcvm.2022.984698. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Echocardiography on day 2 and Chest CT on day 7 in PICU at the age of 6 months. Several Echo variables and ratios indicate severe PH on the second PICU day in acute cardiorespiratory decompensation. Panel (A) shows severe RV hypertrophy and RV dilation. Panel (B) shows increased RV/LV end-systolic diameter ratio of 1.5. Panel (C) shows chest CT with atelectasis of the right upper lobe and mild mosaic perfusion. No signs of cysts or bullae were identified.
in_text_mentions: On day 2 in PICU, transthoracic Echo still showed severe PH with an estimated RVSP of systemic arterial pressure level with a moderately dilated RV and moderate RV systolic dysfunction (Figures 1A,B). The pulmonary artery (PA) was much larger in caliber than the ascending aorta. The left ventricle (LV) appeared underfilled but had normal systolic function. Systemic arterial pressure was 76/46 (mean 61) mmHg. We consequently exchanged epinephrine for norepinephrine, started the ERA macitentan per os, transfused packed red blood cells (PRBC) (goal Hb 12–14 g/dl) and started levosimendan infusion

The patient underwent a chest-computed tomography (CT) already on day 9 in the PICU at the age of 6 months, in order to evaluate the pulmonary parenchyma and vessels (Figure 1C). CT images showed hypoplasia of lung parenchyma with alveolar simplification and diffuse mosaic perfusion, typically associated with extreme premature birth. No cysts or bullae were identified. Additionally, we found an atelectasis of the right upper lobe, which was bronchoscopically flushed out during the same inpatient stay.
